title: How the knight moves
summary: The L-shaped jump: two squares one way, one square sideways; the only piece that jumps.

steps.md: The **knight** moves in an **L**: two squares along a rank or file, then one square to the side. It is the only piece that **jumps**: pieces in between do not matter. Every knight move lands on the **opposite colour**. Value: about 3 pawns.
A knight on d4 reaches eight squares: c6, e6, f5, f3, e2, c2, b3, b5.

steps.explain: Two up (d4-d6), one right (e6). Or think one right, two up: same square.

steps.prompt: Move the knight backwards to c2.
steps.explain: Knights move backwards too. Backward knight moves are among the moves players miss most often.

steps.prompt: Jump over the pawns: move the b1 knight to c3.
steps.explain: The pawns on b2 and c2 are in the way, but knights jump. Only the knights can move before any pawn has moved.

steps.prompt: Bring the knight from a1 to c5 in two moves.
steps.hint: List the knight's two possible first moves and check which one reaches c5.
steps.explain: a1-b3-c5. From the corner the knight has only two moves, b3 and c2, and only b3 leads to c5 in one more jump.

steps.question: A knight stands on a dark square. Where does it land after one move?
steps.explain: Every knight move changes colour. So reaching a square of the same colour always takes an even number of moves.

steps.question: How many moves does a knight in the corner (a1) have, compared with one in the centre (d4)?
steps.explain: "A knight on the rim is dim." Knights need the centre to be effective.

steps.question: Retrieval check: can a knight be blocked by a piece standing next to it?
steps.explain: Only the destination square matters. It must be empty or hold an enemy piece.
